title: Enbridge in talks to sell $1.5-billion pipeline stake to coalition of Indigenous communities
html:
Enbridge Inc. ENB-T is in talks with a consortium of Indigenous communities to sell part of its flagship crude oil pipeline network for roughly $1.5-billion, sources say.

A deal at that valuation would represent the single largest transaction involving Indigenous buyers in Canadian history. More than three dozen First Nation and Métis communities are part of the group that is looking to acquire a minority stake in Enbridge’s Line 3, according to two sources with knowledge of the talks.

The Globe and Mail has agreed not to identify the sources as they are not authorized to discuss details of the confidential discussions.

Code-named “Project Vault,” the proposed deal would involve the consortium paying approximately $1.5-billion for a 6-per-cent stake in Line 3, which carries up to 760,000 barrels of crude oil a day from Edmonton to Superior, Wis. Line 3 is a key component of the Enbridge mainline system, the largest oil pipeline network in North America with the capacity to move up to 3 million barrels a day from Western Canada to refineries across the continent.

The deal is scheduled to be announced in early 2027, the sources said. They added that nothing has been finalized and the exact terms are still subject to change.

Enbridge spokesperson Jesse Semko declined to comment on potential investments in Line 3, but said in an e-mail the company is “currently exploring financial partnerships across numerous assets where the economics are favourable for the Indigenous partners and our business.”

“We see first-hand the value of engaging Indigenous groups as economic partners,” said Mr. Semko. He said Enbridge has struck partnerships valued at more than $2-billion with 65 Indigenous communities in Canada.

Indigenous investments in Canadian pipelines have been growing rapidly in recent years. Between 2021 and early 2026, Indigenous communities acquired ownership interests in more than 5,000 kilometres of operating pipelines across the country, according to data from the Canadian Energy Regulator.

The largest transaction to date occurred in 2022, when Enbridge sold an 11.57 per cent interest in seven pipelines running through northern Alberta to a group of 23 communities for $1.12-billion. In 2025, a consortium of 36 First Nations in B.C. acquired a 12.5 per cent stake in Enbridge’s Westcoast natural gas pipeline network for $715-million.

Most recently, The Globe reported a group of 12 First Nations in northern B.C. is making an investment in TC Energy’s Coastal GasLink pipeline. That deal is expected to be formally announced in Vancouver on Thursday.

In 2022, TC Energy reached equity option agreements with 20 Indigenous communities along Coastal GasLink’s 670-kilometre route.

Many of the latest Indigenous investments have been made possible through the establishment of Indigenous loan guarantee programs at both the provincial and federal levels. Because the federal Indian Act prohibits reserve land from being used as collateral when applying for loans, Indigenous communities have long been forced to pay much higher interest rates on their debt than non-Indigenous borrowers.

Support from programs such as the Canada Indigenous Loan Guarantee Corp. (CILGC) are effectively levelling the playing field, allowing Indigenous communities to access debt closer to market rates. The new sale of part of the Coastal GasLink pipeline was made possible in part by a $168-million CILGC loan guarantee.

The 2025 transaction for a stake in the Enbridge Westcoast network involved a $400-million loan guarantee from CILGC. That was the first deal supported by the young federal Crown corporation, which has up to $10-billion in capacity and is believed to be near the $1-billion threshold already.

Indigenous-led financial institutions such as First Nations Finance Authority (FNFA), Cedar Leaf Capital and First Nations Bank of Canada (FNBC) have also increased the financial resources available to Indigenous communities in recent years.

The Saskatoon-based First Nations Bank closed a $50-million equity financing round earlier this month, which FNBC said will allow it to issue at least $400-million in new commercial loans.

FNFA, meanwhile, has been issuing bonds on behalf of Indigenous communities at a rapidly accelerating pace. Modelled off of the Municipal Finance Authority of B.C., FNFA functions much like a provincial government in the way it accesses debt markets.

It took FNFA a decade to raise $3-billion by issuing a dozen debentures between 2014 and 2024. That total was doubled less than two years later, with FNFA issuing an $840-million bond earlier this month, pushing the total amount of money it has raised beyond $6-billion.

Major banks such as Bank of Montreal and Royal Bank of Canada have also started issuing specialized bonds that directly finance investments that benefit Indigenous peoples. And early next year, Montreal-based fixed-income money manager AlphaFixe Capital Inc. is planning to launch a first-of-its-kind Indigenous reconciliation bond fund.
summary: Deal at that valuation would represent single largest transaction involving Indigenous buyers in Canadian history
